The Trump administration says 9 million barrels a day are still getting out Middle East Iran Welcome to the mega-war: Mideast and European conflicts merge, sucking in more countries along the way—even ones claiming neutrality By Jason Ma Jason Ma Weekend Editor By Jason Ma Jason Ma Weekend Editor August 1, 2026, 1:24 PM ET A U.S. Marine with Battalion Landing Team 3/5, 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit, sights in on a M110 semi-automatic sniper system during a maritime interception operation in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility, July 16, 2026. Add us on Google Add us on Google Wars in Iran and Ukraine are increasingly overlapping while also expanding, as the U.S. mulls whether to make another attempt at delivering a knockout blow against Tehran. Recommended Video Last weekend, Ukraine announced that it attacked an Iranian cargo ship ferrying military supplies between Iran and Russia in the Caspian Sea . Iran insisted it’s not involved in Russia’s war on Ukraine, though Kyiv has said Tehran is supplying drones to its ally. Days later, drones hit liquid natural gas tankers at a port on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, marking the first time the country had been targeted during the Iran war and threatening the Suez Canal’s status as a safe route to get oil out of the Red Sea. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said it formed a military coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea as Iran-backed Houthi rebels attack ships using the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which the kingdom has relied on to export its oil and bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Riyadh said 14 countries offered support for the coalition, including Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria and several other Arab and African nations. Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro, pointed out in a note on Friday that Iran and its allies have struck or threatened nearly every country in the region since the war began in February. “Egypt was the largest one still untouched, and it had worked to stay that way, keeping open relations with both Washington and Tehran,” he added. “Neutrality did not exempt it.” The Mediterranean attack, which Egypt attributed to Iran, may impact European gas prices, shipping rates, and insurance costs, according to Alamariu. That’s as Iran demanded European countries hold Ukraine accountable for its attack on the ship in the Caspian Sea. “The Iran and Ukraine wars may be connecting,” he warned. “A Ukrainian strike in the Caspian Sea was followed within days by burning gas ships on the Mediterranean. It may not be coincidental, there is a tail risk of some convergence between the two conflicts.” Hamidreza Azizi, an Iran expert at the think tank SWP Berlin, also saw potential crosscurrents while laying out different interpretations of Ukraine’s strike on the Iranian ship. One is that Ukraine wants to demonstrate its value as a partner to the U.S., he explained on X last week. Another view is that Israel and the U.S. asked Ukraine to pressure Iran on their behalf amid concerns that any attacks they make on Iranian infrastructure would trigger retaliation against regional economic assets. A third interpretation is that Ukraine’s attack was in response to Houthi rebels threatening ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And according to the Financial Times , Ukraine’s strike prompted speculation in Tehran that it was meant as a warning to demonstrate Iran’s Caspian coast is at risk and could be leveraged in talks with the U.S. Ukraine is already a player in the Middle East, signing a security agreement with Saudi Arabia in March to provide the kingdom with expertise Kyiv has developed in defending against Iranian-designed drones supplied to Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky also made visits to the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to reach similar agreements U.S. Marines assigned to Battalion Landing Team 3/5, 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), conduct weapons drills on a Multi Role-Anti Armor Personnel Weapons System (MAAWS) in the hanger bay of Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Boxer (LHD 4), July 8, 2026. U.S. Navy Former Defense Secretary Mark Esper, who served in the first Trump administration, argued that the Iran war ought to be internationalized to include America’s allies in Asia and Europe as well as countries the border Iran, like Turkey, Armenia and Azerbaijan. “We have to globalize this conflict because it’s affecting international commerce,” he told Bloomberg TV on Thursday. “We’re taking this on too much of ourselves, or to a lesser extent with Israel. So i think it’s time to globalize it and then think about again our broader set of sanctions, blockading the entire country, squeezing them economically.” For its part, Russia is also looking to expand the map. In recent weeks, it has launching drones at Romania while a Russian missile landed in Poland, violating NATO airspace. Russian drones have also crossed into Poland previously, but the latest incident was the first known case involving a Russian missile. The Center for European Policy Analysis said on Friday that the incursions signal that Russia’s “shadow war” against NATO, which has been backing Ukraine, is moving southward . That’s after NATO allies in northern and central Europe saw so-called hybrid war attacks last year, such as the cutting of undersea cables in the Baltic Sea and drone-induced airport closures. Energy expert Daniel Yergin, S&P Global vice chairman, told CNBC on Friday that the Iran war is expanding geographically and geopolitically. “Think about all the seas—the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Baltic Sea, the Caspian Sea—these have all become arenas for oil war,” he said. Skip next section Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack Published 10/20/2026 Published October 20, 2026 last updated 10/20/2026 last updated October 20, 2026 Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack Timothy Jones Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was looking into the theft and subsequent online publication of emails stolen by unidentified hackers during a cyberattack last month. An AfD spokesperson said the hackers had targeted a hosting provider used by the party and appeared to have copied data from a small number of mostly inactive email accounts. "The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded." Although the spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen, an earlier report by the mass-circulation daily Bild put the number of AfD-linked emails published at more than 420,000. According to Bild , the material published included not only emails sent by party figures such as co-leader Alice Weidel but also bank statements, academic certificates and membership lists. The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon. However, archived versions showed a volume of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited." The emails and other materials published have not yet been certified as authentic by any independent body. The AfD, several state chapters of which have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional branches of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has been topping recent national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections . The ZEW's monthly economic confidence index fell to a three-month low on Tuesday, down to 28.1 from 34.7 in September. That is nearly two points lower than forecast. "Private consumption and investment remain weak because of high energy prices: They put real incomes under pressure, increase production costs and keep inflation higher for longer," said ZEW President Achim Wambach. "The German economy," added Wambach, "is slowly emerging from stagnation, but the recovery is not self-sustaining." The biggest losers in this latest index were banks, insurers, the service sector and the telecommunications industry. Winners were seen in the metal manufacturing and electronics industries. ZEW compiles its monthly surveys from interviews with banking, insurance and financial industry experts and businesses on their expectations for economic and capital market developments. The ZEW's index is considered a key indicator for Germany's economic development. Tuesday's survey was based on interviews with 178 analysts between October 12 and 19, 2026. https://p.dw.com/p/5OTYf Skip next section Merz vaunts Germans' 'predictable' character in search of investments 10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 Merz vaunts Germans' 'predictable' character in search of investments Timothy Jones Merz delivered an upbeat and humorous speech in a bid to attract investors Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance Chancellor Friedrich Merz has indulged in an abundance of the most common cliches about his country and compatriots while trying to portray Germany as the ideal place to do business at an investment summit. "Germans are hardworking, going to bed early, rising before dawn," he told the domestic and international guests at the Invest in Germany Summit. "Worst traffic is in the morning between 6 and 7," he said. "On holidays, we are first on the beach, spreading towels before breakfast. If we agree on delivery dates, we stick to it. If you invite friends from Germany for dinner at 7, we will arrive at 6:58. "We are reliable, predictable, precise, and unsurprising," the chancellor continued. "We are, in short, what investors like most." Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil also used blunt humor in his appeal to potential investors, saying in his speech simply: "I want your money." Both pitches appear to have succeeded, with investment commitments worth billions made at the summit. https://p.dw.com/p/5OSzz Skip next section More than €225 billion investment committed at summit — economy minister 10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 More than €225 billion investment committed at summit — economy minister Timothy Jones Economy Minister Katherina Reiche is one of the leading German politicians at the summit Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance More than €225 billion ($252.5 billion) has so far been pledged in investments in Germany at a summit in Berlin attended by top business leaders, German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said on Tuesday. Reiche did not give any details about the commitments made so far, but told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the figure only included deals above a volume of €100 million. Among those planning to invest in Europe's largest economy is online retail giant Amazon, which said it intended to pour some €16 billion into Germany next year for various schemes. The company said these would include "the expansion of data centers and AI infrastructure, high-speed satellite internet through Amazon Leo, new logistics projects across the country, and a major new production slate by Prime Video." "Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe," David Zapolsky, Amazon's chief global affairs and legal officer, was quoted as saying in a statement. "That is why we have invested more than €100 billion here since 2010, and why we plan to invest an additional €16 billion in 2027. We want German businesses, communities, and creators to have the infrastructure and tools they need to compete and grow." More than 200 German and international executives from large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the gathering, entitled the Invest in Germany Summit. https://p.dw.com/p/5OShM Skip next section Left Party debates measures on Israel-critical state parliamentarian 10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 Left Party debates measures on Israel-critical state parliamentarian Timothy Jones Vanessa Emde has made controversial statements criticizing Israel Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance The Left Party in Berlin, which has faced accusations of being antisemitic, is holding a meeting to discuss how to deal with its parliamentarian Vanessa Emde, who has raised controversy with pro-Palestinian statements. Among other things, Emde has supported the idea that there is no right to exist for states, but only for people — thus seemingly going against Germany's firm support of Israel's right to existence. Emde has refused to retract any of her statements. She has also criticized a statement on antisemitism that she had signed along with all other members of the Left's parliamentary party in which the signatories committed to upholding Israel's right to existence. Emde is to attend the online meeting. Greens, SPD agree to coalition negotiations This comes as both the Berlin Green Party and the Social Democrats (SPD) confirmed that they were ready to begin coalition negotiations with the Left Party on forming a joint government in the city-state. The Left Party is due to decide on the issue on October 31 at a party conference. The three parties held preliminary discussions on the accusations of antisemitism and links to organized crime leveled at the Left Party before beginning the exploratory talks that precede final coalition negotiations. The Left Party emerged from September 20 elections in Berlin as the strongest party with 25.7% of the vote. Both the Greens (14.3%) and the center-left SPD (12.1%) came in behind the conservative Christian Democrats (18.8%), who led a previous coalition in Berlin with the SPD. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) received 16.3% of the vote, but so far, all other parties are officially refusing to enter into any form of cooperation with it at either federal or state level. https://p.dw.com/p/5OSYn Skip next section AI cooperation with US' Nvidia announced as investment summit continues 10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 AI cooperation with US' Nvidia announced as investment summit continues Timothy Jones Chancellor Merz is hosting the investment summit Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance The Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin entered its second and final day on Tuesday after opening the previous evening with a speech by Chancellor Friedrich Merz that included the words: "Germany is open for business." The summit has already yielded an agreement to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) in German industry between Germany and US tech giant Nvidia. Merz and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the combination of Germany's engineering expertise and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy over the long term. Merz (L) and Huang announced the cooperation at an opening event Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance More than 200 German and international executives representing large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the event, with closed-door talks scheduled for Tuesday. The summit aims to attract foreign investment to Germany. Organizers highlight the country's sound public finances, triple-A credit rating as the only G7 nation to hold one, strong rule of law and leading position in European patent filings. Despite these advantages, Germany has struggled to attract foreign investment in recent years, with high energy prices and labor costs acting as deterrents. Government sources say investment will be vital to help bridge gaps in public funding as the country seeks to improve infrastructure and support companies' transition to climate-neutral production. Officers have been trying since the early morning to detach the group, a police spokeswoman said. She said as many as 90 officers had been deployed to the site, where altogether 11 protesters were gathered. Rheinmetall is Germany's largest weapons manufacturer. The plant in Wedding, where production began earlier this year, has been the target of several protests , with climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg among those participating. https://p.dw.com/p/5OSFz Skip next section Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens 10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens Timothy Jones German industrial giant Siemens has warned against eliminating entry-level jobs that are now increasingly left to artificial intelligence (AI) , saying young workers could be left without essential skills, including those needed to monitor AI-generated work. Judith Wiese, the company's chief people and sustainability officer, said that handing certain routine tasks to AI meant that young employees would not gain hands-on experience that could benefit them later in their careers. Wiese said it was necessary, for example, for software developers to be able to write their own code so they could critically examine the code produced by AI. "The crucial question is always: What do I need to have done, checked and seen myself to avoid being misled by AI?" she said. However, Wiese said AI could also help employees acquire skills more quickly, while older colleagues could learn from younger ones who had grown up using AI. Wiese said it was still too early to say how AI would impact employment. Noting that Siemens has some 30,000 software engineers, she said: "You can use the additional productivity either to do the same work with fewer people or to do more with the same number of employees." Wiese also pointed out that AI was speeding up work processes, enabling the exploration of new ideas and creating projects that would not have been possible without it. https://p.dw.com/p/5OS9s Skip next section Welcome to our coverage 10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 Welcome to our coverage Timothy Jones | Louis Oelofse Editor DW''s newsroom in Bonn bids a warm guten Tag to all its readers as a previously balmy October decides to move toward more wintry chill.
